claim: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are one of the largest membrane protein families in eukaryotes.
source: One of the largest membrane protein families in eukaryotes are G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about GPCR classification.

claim: GPCRs modulate cell physiology by activating diverse intracellular transducers, prominently heterotrimeric G proteins.
source: GPCRs modulate cell physiology by activating diverse intracellular transducers, prominently heterotrimeric G proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GPCR function.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of rhodopsin in complex with heterotrimeric Gi reveals the receptor C-terminal tail bound to the Gβ subunit.
source: Our density map reveals the receptor C-terminal tail bound to the Gβ subunit of the G protein, providing a structural foundation for the role of the C-terminal tail in GPCR signaling, and of Gβ as scaffold for recruiting Gα subunits and G protein-receptor kinases.
evidence: This is directly supported by the cryo-EM density map data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There are almost 800 GPCR members in humans.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are the most diverse class of integral membrane proteins with almost 800 members in humans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the number of human GPCRs.

claim: GPCRs are activated by a great diversity of extracellular stimuli including photons, neurotransmitters, ions, proteins, and hormones.
source: GPCRs are activated by a great diversity of extracellular stimuli including photons, neurotransmitters, ions, proteins, and hormones (Glukhova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Upon activation, GPCRs couple to intracellular transducers, including four subtypes of G proteins (Gαs, Gαi/o, Gαq/11, Gα12/13).
source: Upon activation, GPCRs couple to intracellular transducers, including four subtypes of G proteins (Gαs, Gαi/o, Gαq/11, Gα12/13) (Milligan and Kostenis, 2006), seven subtypes of GPCR kinases (GRKs) (Gurevich et al., 2012), and four subtypes of arrestins (Smith and Rajagopal, 2016) (Figure 1A), among many other partners (Magalhaes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most GPCRs are promiscuous and can couple to more than one G protein subtype.
source: While most GPCRs are promiscuous and can couple to more than one G protein subtype (Flock et al., 2017), the molecular determinants of G protein recognition are not yet fully understood.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The molecular determinants of G protein recognition are not yet fully understood.
source: While most GPCRs are promiscuous and can couple to more than one G protein subtype (Flock et al., 2017), the molecular determinants of G protein recognition are not yet fully understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Understanding the molecular basis for G protein coupling and selectivity could lead to the design of drugs that promote specific signaling pathways and avoid unwanted side effects.
source: Understanding the molecular basis for G protein coupling and selectivity could lead to the design of drugs that promote specific signaling pathways and avoid unwanted side effects (Hauser et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications, supported by a citation.

claim: Out of the 13 structures of GPCR-G protein complexes available, six contain a Gi/o subtype.
source: Out of the 13 structures of GPCR-G protein complexes available, six contain a Gi/o subtype: μ-opioid receptor bound to Gi (Koehl et al., 2018), adenosine A1 receptor bound to Gi (Draper-Joyce et al., 2018), cannabinoid receptor one bound to Gi (Krishna Kumar et al., 2019), human rhodopsin bound to Gi (Kang et al., 2018), 5HT1B receptor bound to Go (García-Nafría et al., 2018b), and bovine rhodopsin bound to an engineered Go (mini-Go) (Tsai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior structures.

claim: The preparation of GPCR-G protein complexes for structural biology remains challenging.
source: However, the preparation of GPCR-G protein complexes for structural biology still remains challenging (Munk et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Nanobodies, Fab fragments, and mini-G proteins have been very important tools to overcome the inherent instability and flexibility of GPCR-G protein complexes and obtain near atomic-resolution structures.
source: Nanobodies (Rasmussen et al., 2011), Fab fragments (Kang et al., 2018; Koehl et al., 2018), and mini-G proteins (García-Nafría et al., 2018b; Tsai et al., 2018) have been very important tools to overcome the inherent instability and flexibility of these complexes and obtain near atomic-resolution structures.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Rhodopsin has been shown to interact with the Gβγ subunit of the G protein heterotrimer to assist binding and activation of the Gα subunit.
source: Rhodopsin has been shown to interact with the Gβγ subunit of the G protein heterotrimer to assist binding and activation of the Gα subunit (Herrmann et al., 2004; Herrmann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A direct interaction between rhodopsin and Gβγ could not be observed in the existing complex structure by Kang et al., 2018.
source: Despite this biochemical evidence, a direct interaction between rhodopsin and Gβγ could not be observed in the existing complex (Kang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about what was not observed in a prior structure, supported by citation.

claim: The overall structure of the rhodopsin-Gi-Fab16 complex agrees well with current published structures.
source: Overall, our structure agrees well with current published structures (Kang et al., 2018; Tsai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cited structures.

claim: The EM density map shows that intracellular loops 2 and 3 of rhodopsin are at contact distance to Gα.
source: The density map also shows that intracellular loops (ICL) 2 and 3 of rhodopsin are at contact distance to Gα.
evidence: This is directly supported by the EM density map data.

claim: The rhodopsin-Gi complex was reconstituted in the detergent lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) in presence of Fab16.
source: We reconstituted the rhodopsin-Gαi1β1γ1 complex in the detergent lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) (Maeda et al., 2014) in presence of Fab16 (Maeda et al., 2018) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), as cryo-EM screening revealed that the complex without Fab could not be refined to high resolution (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: The complex without Fab could not be refined to high resolution.
source: We reconstituted the rhodopsin-Gαi1β1γ1 complex in the detergent lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) (Maeda et al., 2014) in presence of Fab16 (Maeda et al., 2018) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), as cryo-EM screening revealed that the complex without Fab could not be refined to high resolution (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: 3D classification revealed that the density corresponding to Gα is heterogeneous.
source: During image processing (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4), 3D classification revealed that the density corresponding to Gα is heterogeneous (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), particularly at flexible regions such as the α-helical (AH) domain.
evidence: This is supported by the image processing data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The final map has a nominal global resolution of 4.38 Å.
source: The AH domain was then excluded by using a soft mask during refinement, resulting in a map with a nominal global resolution of 4.38 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in supplementary figures.

claim: The cryo-EM structure is in excellent agreement with the crystal structure of the same rhodopsin mutant bound to a mini-Go protein.
source: In particular, our cryo-EM structure is in excellent agreement with the crystal structure of the same rhodopsin mutant bound to a mini-Go protein (Tsai et al., 2018), with a nearly identical orientation of the C-terminal α5 helix (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B), which contacts transmembrane helices (TM) 2, 3, 5–7 and the TM7/helix 8 (H8) turn of the receptor (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to a cited structure and data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The EM map reveals a density on the Gβ subunit as continuation of H8 of the receptor, which corresponds to the C-tail of rhodopsin.
source: The EM map reveals a density on the Gβ subunit as continuation of H8 of the receptor (Figure 2A), which corresponds to the C-tail of rhodopsin.
evidence: This is directly supported by the EM density map data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: This feature of the C-tail binding to Gβ has only been observed in the recent structure of the M1 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor in complex with G11.
source: This feature has only been observed in the recent structure of the M1 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor in complex with G11 (Maeda et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent structure.

claim: Half of the C-tail of rhodopsin (12 out of 25 residues; 324–335) was modeled into the density as a continuous stretched peptide.
source: We modeled half of the C-tail of rhodopsin (12 out of 25 residues; 324–335) into this density as a continuous stretched peptide with residues G324, P327 and G329 serving as flexible hinges (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the modeling process based on the density map data.

claim: In the inactive state, the C-tail folds around the cytoplasmic side of rhodopsin, although this is likely due to crystal packing as this region is intrinsically disordered in the absence of a binding partner.
source: In the inactive state, the C-tail folds around the cytoplasmic side of rhodopsin, although this is likely due to crystal packing as this region is intrinsically disordered in the absence of a binding partner (Jaakola et al., 2005; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the G protein complex, the C-tail stretches over a polar surface on the cleft between Gα and Gβ, interacting with both subunits.
source: In our G protein complex, the C-tail stretches over a polar surface on the cleft between Gα and Gβ, interacting with both subunits (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In Gβ, the interacting residues are C271, D290, and D291 in blade six and R314 in blade 7 of the β-propeller.
source: In Gβ, the interacting residues are C271, D290, and D291 in blade six and R314 in blade 7 of the β-propeller (Figure 2D), which impart a local negative electrostatic potential (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural data and analysis shown in figures.

claim: The interacting residues C271, D290, D291, and R314 in Gβ are conserved in Gβ1–4 but not in Gβ5.
source: These residues are conserved in Gβ1–4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) but not in Gβ5, the least similar to the other Gβ subtypes (Dupré et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in supplementary figures and a citation.

claim: In Gα, the interacting residues with the C-tail are N256H3.15 and K257H3.16 in helix 3 of the Ras domain.
source: In Gα, the interacting residues with the C-tail are N256H3.15 and K257H3.16 in helix 3 of the Ras domain (Figure 2D), which confer instead a local positive electrostatic potential (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural data and analysis shown in figures.

claim: The residues N256H3.15 and K257H3.16 in Gα are quite conserved across G protein subtypes except Gq.
source: These residues are quite conserved across G protein subtypes except Gq (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The regions in Gα and Gβ that contact the receptor C-tail are also involved in recognition of GRK2.
source: Interestingly, these regions in Gα and Gβ that contact the receptor C-tail are also involved in recognition of GRK2 (Tesmer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the rhodopsin-arrestin complex, part of the proximal segment of the C-terminus (residues 325–329) is not resolved, but the distal part could be modeled up to S343.
source: In the rhodopsin-arrestin complex part of the proximal segment of the C-terminus (residues 325–329) is not resolved, but the distal part could be modeled up to S343, eight residues longer than in our G protein complex and including two phosphorylated sites.
evidence: This is based on comparison to a prior arrestin-bound structure.

claim: In the presence of arrestin, the C-tail stretches further, with residues K339-T342 forming a short β-strand antiparallel to the N-terminal β-strand of arrestin.
source: In the presence of arrestin, the C-tail stretches further, with residues K339-T342 forming a short β-strand antiparallel to the N-terminal β-strand of arrestin (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on comparison to a prior arrestin-bound structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Distinct portions of the C-tail are responsible for contacting different intracellular partners.
source: Thus, it appears that distinct portions of the C-tail are responsible for contacting different intracellular partners.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparisons presented.

claim: The central part of the C-tail (residues 330–335) can bind to Gα and Gβ.
source: The central part of the C-tail (residues 330–335) can bind to Gα and Gβ, while the distal half of the C-tail (residues 336–343), which contains five (out of six) phosphorylation sites (Azevedo et al., 2015), binds to arrestin (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and comparison to arrestin-bound structures.

claim: The distal half of the C-tail (residues 336–343) contains five out of six phosphorylation sites and binds to arrestin.
source: The central part of the C-tail (residues 330–335) can bind to Gα and Gβ, while the distal half of the C-tail (residues 336–343), which contains five (out of six) phosphorylation sites (Azevedo et al., 2015), binds to arrestin (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and a citation about phosphorylation sites.

claim: The C-terminal α5 helix of Gα forms the major contact interface to rhodopsin.
source: As in the other existing GPCR-G protein complex structures, the C-terminal α5 helix of Gα forms the major contact interface to rhodopsin.
evidence: This is based on comparison to other GPCR-G protein structures.

claim: The majority of the contacts formed by the α5 helix to GPCRs concentrate in the region from H5.11 to H5.26.
source: The majority of the contacts formed by the α5 helix to GPCRs concentrate in the region from H5.11 to H5.26 (Glukhova et al., 2018) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The main contacts to the α5 helix are formed by TM5 and TM6, followed by TM3 and TM7/8.
source: We compiled an exhaustive list of the residue-residue contacts between the receptor and the α5 helix in all the available GPCR/G protein complexes, and observed that the main contacts to the α5 helix are formed by TM5 and TM6, followed by TM3 and TM7/8 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by comprehensive analysis of multiple structures shown in figures.

claim: In all Gi complexes, PheH5.26 and GlyH5.24 contact TM6 and TM7/H8 of the receptor, respectively.
source: Thus, our analysis suggests that ICL2 and ICL3 contribute to the binding interface between receptor and G protein, a feature that may be required to further stabilize the complex during nucleotide exchange.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis presented.

claim: In all Gs complexes, LeuH5.26, ArgH5.17 and ArgH5.12 contact TM5/ICL3, TM5, and TM3/ICL2, respectively.
source: However, at the interface between receptor and the α5 helix of the G protein, in all Gi complexes PheH5.26 and GlyH5.24 contact TM6 and TM7/H8 of the receptor, respectively. Instead, in all Gs complexes we find that LeuH5.26, ArgH5.17 and ArgH5.12 contact TM5/ICL3, TM5, and TM3/ICL2, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by comprehensive analysis of multiple structures.

claim: ArgH5.17 appears to consistently interact with residue 5.68 in class A GPCRs, and with Lys5.64 in class B GPCRs.
source: Interestingly, ArgH5.17 appears to consistently interact with residue 5.68 in class A GPCRs, and with Lys5.64 in class B GPCRs (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in figures.

claim: A tight interaction between ArgH5.17 and TM5 might be one of the main determinants for the Gs-specific relocation of TM6.
source: We suggest that a tight interaction between ArgH5.17 and TM5 might be one of the main determinants for the Gs-specific relocation of TM6.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural data.

claim: ICL2 lies near αN/β1 and β2/β3 of Gα in all analyzed structures.
source: In all analyzed structures, we found that ICL2 lies near αN/β1 and β2/β3 of Gα, while ICL3 is close to α4/β6 (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: ICL3 is close to α4/β6 of Gα in all analyzed structures.
source: In all analyzed structures, we found that ICL2 lies near αN/β1 and β2/β3 of Gα, while ICL3 is close to α4/β6 (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: ICL2 folds into an α-helical structure in all the class A receptors except rhodopsin.
source: Interestingly, ICL2 folds into an α-helical structure in all the class A receptors except rhodopsin (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in supplementary figures.

claim: ICL2 does not contribute to binding Gα in the structures of 5HT1B-mini-Go and A1AR-Gi.
source: ICL2 does not contribute to binding Gα in the structures of 5HT1B-mini-Go and A1AR-Gi.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of specific complexes.

claim: The contact between Gα and ICL2 discriminates between class A GPCRs (which interact via the αN/β1 loop) and class B GPCRs (which interact via the region around β1 and β2/β3).
source: Nevertheless, the contact between Gα and ICL2 seems to discriminate between class A GPCRs –which interact via the αN/β1 loop– and class B GPCRs –which instead the region around β1 and β2/β3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: ICL3 is one of the most diverse regions in GPCRs and is often not completely resolved in the available structures.
source: ICL3, one of the most diverse regions in GPCRs, is often not completely resolved in the available structures (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D), either because it is too flexible or because it has been engineered to facilitate structural determination (Munk et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by structural observations and a citation.

claim: Gi/o-coupled receptors use residues on TM5/ICL3/TM6 to contact the α4/β6 region, while Gs-coupled receptors mainly use TM5/ICL3.
source: Gi/o-coupled receptors use residues on TM5/ICL3/TM6 to contact the α4/β6 region, while Gs-coupled receptors mainly use TM5/ICL3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The difference in ICL3 contacts between Gi/o and Gs complexes is due to the larger displacement of TM6 in Gs complexes.
source: This difference is due to the larger displacement of TM6 in Gs complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis.

claim: Residue TyrG.S6.02 in ICL3, highly conserved in all G protein subtypes, engages the receptor in about half of all the complexes.
source: In ICL3, residue TyrG.S6.02, highly conserved in all G protein subtypes, engages the receptor in about half of all the complexes.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis across multiple complexes.

claim: TyrG.S6.02 has been shown to be crucial for the stabilization of the rhodopsin-Gi complex.
source: This residue has been shown to be crucial for the stabilization of the rhodopsin-Gi complex (Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ICL2 and ICL3 contribute to the binding interface between receptor and G protein, which may be required to further stabilize the complex during nucleotide exchange.
source: Thus, our analysis suggests that ICL2 and ICL3 contribute to the binding interface between receptor and G protein, a feature that may be required to further stabilize the complex during nucleotide exchange.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural analysis.

claim: The binding mode of the G protein Ras domain is virtually identical to the previously reported X-ray structure of the same receptor bound to a mini-Go protein.
source: In particular, we found that the binding mode of the G protein Ras domain –including the key C-terminal α5 helix– is virtually identical to our previously reported X-ray structure of the same receptor bound to a mini-Go protein (Tsai et al., 2018) (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to a prior structure and data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The unique combination of a full-length C-tail, Gβγ purified from bovine rod outer segments, and Fab16 may have contributed to trap the transient interaction of the intrinsically disordered C-tail to Gβ.
source: Thus, our bovine rhodopsin complex contains the unique combination of a full-length C-tail, Gβγ purified from bovine rod outer segments, and Fab16 that may have contributed to trap the transient interaction of the intrinsically disordered C-tail to Gβ.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about why the C-tail was observed in this structure.

claim: The recently published structure of the M1 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor in complex with G11 and scFv16 reveals part of the receptor C-tail bound to the G protein in essentially the same conformation as in the rhodopsin-Gi structure.
source: Remarkably, the recently published structure of the M1 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor in complex with G11 and scFv16 (Maeda et al., 2019) reveals part of the receptor C-tail bound to the G protein in essentially the same conformation as in our structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to a recently published structure.

claim: The Gβγ subunit engages with a wide range of effectors.
source: The Gβγ subunit engages with a wide range of effectors (Dupré et al., 2009; Khan et al., 2013), including direct interactions with GPCRs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GPCRs can associate with Gβγ prior to trafficking to the plasma membrane.
source: For instance, these can associate prior to trafficking to the plasma membrane (Dupré et al., 2006) where they can remain pre-coupled (Galés et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: According to a sequential fit model, activated rhodopsin binds to Gβγ assisting to position the Ras domain of Gα into proximity of its binding site to the receptor.
source: Also, according to a sequential fit model (Herrmann et al., 2004; Herrmann et al., 2006), activated rhodopsin binds to Gβγ assisting to position the Ras domain of Gα into proximity of its binding site to the receptor.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The positioning of Gα by Gβγ would facilitate folding of the C-terminal α5 helix of Gα leading to nucleotide exchange.
source: This would facilitate folding of the C-terminal α5 helix of this subunit leading to nucleotide exchange (Dror et al., 2015; Flock et al., 2015; Kapoor et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HEK cells lacking functional Gα subunits (but retaining the native Gβγ) are still able to recruit arrestin, although they fail to activate ERK and whole-cell responses.
source: Interestingly, HEK cells lacking functional Gα subunits (but retaining the native Gβγ) are still able to recruit arrestin, although they fail to activate ERK and whole-cell responses (Grundmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The observed interaction between the central part of the receptor C-terminus and Gβγ is involved in localizing the G protein heterotrimer to the active receptor first.
source: Our findings provide a structural explanation for these roles of Gβγ in GPCR-mediated signaling. We suggest that the observed interaction between the central part of the receptor C-terminus and Gβγ is involved in localizing the G protein heterotrimer to the active receptor first.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural findings.

claim: After dissociation of the Gα subunit, a transient Gβγ/receptor complex could provide the adequate molecular context to allow receptor phosphorylation by bringing the kinase close to the receptor C-tail.
source: After dissociation of the Gα subunit, a transient Gβγ/receptor complex could provide the adequate molecular context to allow receptor phosphorylation by bringing the kinase close to the receptor C-tail (Ribas et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: In other class A GPCRs, interactions with Gβγ have been located in ICL3 (in M2 and M3 muscarinic receptors) and potentially in ICL1 (in A2AR and β2AR).
source: In other class A GPCRs, interactions with Gβγ have been also located in ICL3 (in M2 and M3) muscarinic receptors, involved in the phosphorylation of this loop (Wu et al., 1998) and potentially in ICL1 (in A2AR and β2AR) (García-Nafría et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the rhodopsin-Gi complex, K6612.48 and K6712.49 in ICL1 are close to D312 in Gβ (7 Å between Cα atoms), but no defined density for the side chains is observed in this region.
source: In our complex, K6612.48 and K6712.49 in ICL1 are indeed close to D312 in Gβ (7 Å between Cα atoms); however, we do not observe defined density for the side chains in this region (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and density map observations.

claim: The complexes of the class B GPCRs calcitonin and GLP-1 feature an extended and tilted H8 resulting in extensive contacts with Gβγ that have not been observed in Class A receptors.
source: Interestingly, the complexes of the class B GPCRs calcitonin and GLP-1 feature an extended and tilted H8 resulting in extensive contacts with Gβγ that have not been observed in Class A receptors (García-Nafría et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: H8 has been shown to bind Gβγ in the class B PTH1 receptor.
source: H8 has also been shown to bind Gβγ in the class B PTH1 receptor (Mahon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Class A and class B GPCRs likely use distinct mechanisms to engage Gβγ.
source: Thus, it is likely that class A and class B GPCRs use distinct mechanisms to engage Gβγ.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural differences observed between class A and class B receptors.

claim: The receptor-Gβγ interaction observed in the rhodopsin-Gi structure is compatible with proposed models of receptor-GRK recognition.
source: The receptor-Gβγ interaction observed in our structure is compatible with proposed models of receptor-GRK recognition (Komolov et al., 2017; Sarnago et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The Gβγ subunit can 'tag' activated GPCRs and provide an interface for bringing different effectors (Gα subunits first, and GRKs later) near the cytoplasmic domains of GPCRs.
source: Thus, we suggest that the Gβγ subunit can 'tag' activated GPCRs and provide an interface for bringing different effectors (Gα subunits first, and GRKs later) near the cytoplasmic domains of GPCRs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural findings.

claim: The conserved contacts identified between α5 and the receptors are structurally important anchoring points.
source: While our analysis is limited by the number of available structures, we suggest that the conserved contacts identified between α5 and the receptors are structurally important anchoring points, but we cannot exclude that they might be relevant at the level of recognition between G protein subtypes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural analysis.

claim: More work on the structural characterization of complexes is needed to visualize snapshots of the signaling pathway that have not been observed yet.
source: In order to visualize snapshots of the signaling pathway that have not been observed yet, more work on the structural characterization of complexes is still needed, ideally using the same receptor and different transducers.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: The constitutively active mutant of bovine rhodopsin N2C/M257Y/D282C binds to the Gi protein heterotrimer.
source: To obtain a rhodopsin-Gi complex suitable for structural studies, we expressed in HEK cells the constitutively active mutant of bovine rhodopsin N2C/M257Y/D282C (Deupi et al., 2012) which binds to the Gi protein heterotrimer (Maeda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The Gβ1γ1 subunit was isolated from bovine retinae and contains native post-translational modification important for transducin function.
source: The Gβ1γ1 subunit was isolated from bovine retinae and thus contains native post-translational modification important for transducin function (Matsuda and Fukada, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The cryo-EM density map is deposited under accession code EMD-4598 on the EM Data Bank.
source: The cryo-EM density map is deposited under accession code EMD-4598 on the EM Data Bank.
evidence: This is a statement about data deposition.

claim: The structure coordinates of the rhodopsin-complex bound to Fab16 are deposited under accession code 6QNO on the Protein Data Bank.
source: The related structure coordinates of the rhodopsin-complex bound to Fab16 (accession code 6QNO) and the crystal structure of Fab16 (accession code 6QNK) are deposited on the Protein Data Bank.
evidence: This is a statement about data deposition.

claim: The crystal structure of Fab16 is deposited under accession code 6QNK on the Protein Data Bank.
source: The related structure coordinates of the rhodopsin-complex bound to Fab16 (accession code 6QNO) and the crystal structure of Fab16 (accession code 6QNK) are deposited on the Protein Data Bank.
evidence: This is a statement about data deposition.
